## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Manga (`lumenary:manga`, a style that rests on this process)

_From: Japanese comics; when: Screentone in manga since the 1960s; works best on: Portraits in strong light; pictures with a clear subject._

A comic page is printed in black ink on white paper, so every shade has to be built from marks. Manga artists do it with screentone: a sheet of tiny dots or lines stuck on the page and cut away where it is not wanted. Fine dots read as a pale grey, coarse dots as a mid grey, hatching as a darker one. The few marks still carry light, shape and mood, and the speed lines say where the eye should go.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Lift the local contrast, so that faces and folds keep their shape when only a few tones are left.
2. Cut the tone into bands: bare paper, fine dots, coarse dots, hatching, cross-hatching and solid black.
3. Fill each band with a screentone of its own, laid at 45 degrees and anti-aliased.
4. Find the ink line where the tone changes fast, and add thin dark features such as eyes and creases.
5. Optionally add speed lines, only in flat, light places, and a pale wash of the picture’s colour beneath it all.
6. Finish with paper grain and a black panel frame.

**The maths:**

$$T=\ell+0.9\,(\ell-\bar\ell)$$

_Local contrast: l is the brightness and its bar a wide blur._ (primitives: unsharp-mask)

$$u=\frac{x+y}{\sqrt2\,p},\quad v=\frac{x-y}{\sqrt2\,p},\qquad c=\operatorname{clamp}\Big(\big(\sqrt{\delta/\pi}-\sqrt{\Delta u^{2}+\Delta v^{2}}\big)\,p+\tfrac12\Big)$$

_A screentone dot: du and dv are the offsets from the nearest lattice point, and delta the share of the cell that is inked._ (primitives: tone-dot-lattice)

$$\text{ink}=\max\Big(\text{tone},\ \text{rays}\cdot S_{0.58,0.72}(T)\big(1-S_{0.018,0.06}(\overline{|\nabla T|})\big),\ \text{line}\Big)$$

_Speed lines fill only light, flat places; the outline is drawn over everything. S is smoothstep._ (primitives: soft-threshold, image-gradient)

**Dials:** `tone` (Size of the screentone) = 100 [40 to 200]; `line` (Ink outline) = 55 [0 to 100]; `black` (Solid black) = 45 [0 to 100]; `speed` (Speed lines) = "none" (none, focus, rush); `wash` (Colour) = "bw" (bw, wash); `paper` (Paper) = "white" (white, cream); `panel` (Panel frame) = true; `seed` (Another page) = 1.

**History:** Modern manga took shape in the postwar years with Osamu Tezuka, whose cinematic panels and large-eyed faces set the style from 1947. Early pages were shaded by hand with ink. From the 1960s, adhesive sheets printed with dots and lines, cut to shape with a craft knife and pressed onto the page, let artists cover large areas quickly, and by the 1980s there were hundreds of patterns to choose from. Today most tone is laid digitally, but the dot patterns are the same ones.
